prompt.context: Our client is a coffin maker in the Eastern European country of Maldovia. He has seen substantial change in his market in recent years and is contemplating the future of his business. Up until now, he has been in the business of building high-quality, hand-crafted coffins largely by hand with a skilled labor force. Recently, however, he has become aware of technology that would allow him to build machine-made coffins with much less labor.
prompt.question: Should he invest in this new technology, and should he even remain in the coffin business in the first place? What strategic alternatives should the owner consider?

clarifying_info.q: What is the population of Maldovia and relevant demographic data?
clarifying_info.a: Population: 4 million. Population growth: 0%. Life expectancy: 75 years. Age distribution is flat (same number of people at every age). 75% of deaths are buried in coffins.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current price and cost structure?
clarifying_info.a: Coffins are priced at $5,000 for a hand-made coffin. COGS is $4,800 per coffin (material is 10% of direct cost, labor is 90%). Fixed costs are $700,000 per year. All assets are fully depreciated; ignore taxes.

clarifying_info.q: What is the company's market share?
clarifying_info.a: Maldovian Coffins has 10% market share and a relative market share of approximately 1 (the ratio of the company's market share to that of its nearest competitor).

clarifying_info.q: What are the market trends, regulation, and external factors?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the market is expected to continue as it currently is.

clarifying_info.q: What would the new technology investment cost, and what savings does it generate?
clarifying_info.a: Investing in the new technology will cost $1 million. Material costs remain the same, but labor costs are reduced by 50%.

clarifying_info.q: Is the technology proprietary or exclusive to our client?
clarifying_info.a: The technology is currently offered for sale by a machine tool company that holds the patent. They are not offering exclusivity — they will sell to competitors as well.

clarifying_info.q: Will customers prefer hand-made over machine-made coffins?
clarifying_info.a: The quality perceived by the customer is the same or better. The customer is expected to be indifferent between hand-made and machine-made coffins. Brand impact is negligible.

clarifying_info.q: What are the fixed assets of the business?
clarifying_info.a: Since the firm builds coffins by hand, fixed assets are essentially only land and improvements. The company owns these assets outright. Book value of land: $20,000. Book value of improvements: $80,000. The property has been owned for 48 years. Average real estate appreciation: 6% per year.

framework: Define the strategic options: (1) Sell the business to a third party, (2) Liquidate assets and shut down, (3) Keep operating as-is, (4) Keep operating and invest in new technology
Calculate the current value of the business as a going concern (discounted cash flows / perpetuity)
Calculate the liquidation value (sell the land and improvements at appreciated market value)
Calculate the value if the new technology is adopted, accounting for competitive dynamics and likely price erosion
Compare all four options and recommend the highest-value path

questions.prompt: Calculate the size of the Maldovian coffin market (number of coffins purchased per year).
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that with a flat age distribution, 1/75th of the population turns 76 and dies each year. Apply the 75% burial rate to get coffins demanded. Strong candidates also brainstorm multiple ways to estimate market size before being given the data.

math.setup: Deaths per year = Population / Life Expectancy = 4,000,000 / 75. Coffins = Deaths x Burial Rate.

questions.prompt: What is the current value of the business as a going concern?
questions.guidance: Candidate calculates contribution margin, subtracts fixed costs to get annual profit, then values as a perpetuity. Should state an assumed discount rate (10% is standard) and apply it consistently.

math.setup: Contribution margin per coffin = Price - COGS = $5,000 - $4,800 = $200. Company volume = Market x Share. Annual profit = CM total - Fixed Costs. Value = Profit / Discount Rate.

questions.prompt: What is the liquidation value of the business (sell the land and improvements)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm ways to value the property (comparable sales, rental cash flow discounting, appreciation from book value). Then use the rule of 72 to calculate current market value. Compare to going-concern value.

math.setup: Total book value = $20,000 + $80,000 = $100,000. Rule of 72: doubling period = 72 / 6% = 12 years. Held for 48 years = 4 doubling periods. Current value = $100,000 x 2^4.
math.answer: $1.6 million — liquidation value exceeds going-concern value of $1M, so selling the assets is more attractive than continuing to operate as-is

questions.prompt: What would the value of the company be if the owner invests in the new technology? Account for competitive dynamics.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize that because the technology is non-proprietary, competitors can and likely will adopt it too. This drives industry-wide cost reduction and ultimately price reduction. Assume gross margins stay constant (competitive equilibrium). Candidate should calculate new price, new CM, and resulting profit/loss. The business becomes unprofitable, reinforcing the recommendation to liquidate.

math.setup: Current gross margin = $200/$5,000 = 4%. New labor cost = ($4,800 x 90%) x 50%. New COGS = new labor + material. New price = New COGS / (1 - gross margin%). New CM = New price - New COGS. New annual profit = CM x volume - Fixed Costs.
steps: Original labor cost = $4,800 x 90% = $4,320; after 50% reduction = $2,160
New price (keeping 4% gross margin) = $2,640 / (1 - 0.04) = $2,640 / 0.96 = $2,750 (approximately $2,718 as stated in casebook)
math.answer: Annual loss of approximately $388,000; business is unprofitable under the new technology scenario if competitors also adopt it

brainstorming.prompt: What are the different ways to determine the size of the Maldovian coffin market?

categories.name: Population-based estimates
ideas: Calculate from population, life expectancy, and flat age distribution (1/75th die each year)
Calculate from population growth rate and birth rate to estimate annual cohort aging out
Use total population and average life expectancy to derive annual death rate

categories.name: Record-based methods
ideas: Review death records for a period of time and aggregate
Take a sample of obituaries in local newspapers serving a given population base
Survey funeral homes on annual coffin purchases

categories.name: Real estate / comparables
ideas: Look for comparable data from similar Eastern European countries with known burial customs
Check industry association reports on coffin sales volumes

recommendation: The owner should liquidate the business and sell the assets rather than continue operating or invest in the new technology
Liquidation value of $1.6M (appreciated land and improvements) exceeds the going-concern value of $1M and the technology investment scenario which results in operating losses
risks: If real estate appreciation assumptions are wrong, liquidation value could be lower than estimated
If competitors do NOT adopt the technology, margins under the new technology could be maintained at higher levels than modeled
Brand loyalty or local market dynamics could support higher-than-industry-average pricing
next_steps: Conduct a formal real estate appraisal of the land and improvements to validate the $1.6M estimate
Explore whether competitors have plans to adopt the new technology to stress-test the price erosion assumption
Evaluate potential buyers for the business as a going concern vs. asset sale to determine which exit path maximizes proceeds
